title: The loan-approval assistant
kicker: World 7 · Decide Where It Matters · Boss

job.text:
New domain, held out. A loan-approval assistant runs five steps. Tier every step by the cost of being wrong, hard-gate the steps that must be exact, and send the high-stakes judgment to a person.

Boss rule: the real ask is free text — "tier every step by cost of being wrong; hard-gate the exact ones; name who owns the riskiest decision." For now you build that ask from the chips below; your pass is decided by the hidden expert key, never by the AI's say-so. Two new tricks are on the table — resist both.

rows: Look up the current rate from the rate sheet

naivePrompt: Automate the whole thing for speed.
basePrompt: Automate the whole thing for speed.

text.plain: Hard-gate the debt-to-income score — it has exactly one right answer, so a tool must compute it.
text.tech: Mark step 1 (DTI score) gate: hard; attach a calculator that must match exactly.

text.plain: Hard-gate the rate lookup — the rate comes from the rate sheet, so a tool must read it, not guess it.
text.tech: Mark step 2 (rate) gate: hard; the value is read from the rate sheet by a lookup.

text.plain: Send the final approval or denial to a human — it's the highest-cost judgment in the workflow.
text.tech: Mark step 5 (final decision) gate: human; a reviewer signs off before any approval or denial.

text.plain: Hard-gate the approval-letter wording — but wording has no single right answer to gate against.
text.tech: Mark step 3 (letter wording) gate: hard — but it is open-ended text.

moves.label: Automate the final decision for speed

text.plain: Let the assistant approve or deny on its own to go faster — but a wrongful approval or denial is the costliest error here.
text.tech: Mark step 5 (final decision) gate: heuristic — but automating the highest-stakes judgment ships wrongful decisions.

moves.label: Let the model decide the rate

text.plain: Let the model pick the rate instead of reading the rate sheet — but then the quoted rate is a guess.
text.tech: Mark step 2 (rate) gate: heuristic and let the model produce it — but the rate must come from the sheet.

rules.claim: The final decision was automated for speed — and the assistant approved a loan it shouldn't have.
rules.feedback: The costliest call went to the guesser. Approving or denying a loan is the highest-stakes judgment here — "automate it all for speed" ships wrongful decisions. That step is a human review.
rules.lesson: The highest-cost judgment goes to a human, not to speed.

output.source: the final decision automated for speed

rules.claim: The model picked the rate instead of reading the rate sheet — and quoted a rate that isn't on it.
rules.feedback: You let the model guess the rate. The rate is written on the rate sheet — a lookup has one right value. Letting the model decide it quotes a number that isn't there. Keep that gate hard.
rules.lesson: A right-answer lookup is never the model's to decide.

cells: quoted a rate not on the sheet

output.source: the rate left to the model

rules.claim: A hard gate was put on the letter wording — it caught nothing and slowed the pipeline.
rules.feedback: Over-gated. The approval-letter wording has no single right answer — a hard gate on it catches nothing and just costs time. That step is heuristic.

output.source: a hard gate on an open-ended step

rules.claim: Score and rate → hard gates (exact). Letter and greeting → heuristic. Final decision → a human.
rules.feedback: Right tier for every step. The eligibility score and the rate are gated hard, the open steps run loose, and the costliest judgment — the approval itself — goes to a person. That's the Architect's call.
rules.lesson: Tier by whether it's exact and by the cost of being wrong.

output.source: the hidden expert key for this workflow

rules.claim: A right-answer step was left to the model, or the final decision had no human on it.
rules.feedback: Not tiered yet. The debt-to-income score and the rate each have one right answer — hard-gate both — and the final approval is a high-cost judgment that needs a human. Match the tier to the cost of being wrong.
rules.lesson: Exact steps are hard gates; the costliest judgment is a human's.

hints.nudge: For each step, ask who gets hurt and how badly if it's wrong.
hints.gap: Two steps are exact calculations or lookups — those are hard gates. One step is the costliest judgment — that's a human's.
hints.moves: Hard-gate the debt-to-income score and the rate lookup; send the final approval or denial to a human. Leave the letter wording and the greeting on heuristic — and don't automate the decision or let the model pick the rate.

whatYouDoDifferently.naive: Automate the whole thing → a wrongful approval ships and the rate is a guess.
whatYouDoDifferently.rewrite: Hard-gate the score and the rate, leave the wording loose, send the decision to a person.

template.plain: New workflow. For each step, tell me the cost of being wrong and bucket it: must be exact (tool-gated) / best-effort / human decides. Hard-gate every exact step, and name who owns the riskiest decision.
template.tech: New workflow. For each step annotate gate: hard | heuristic | human from cost-of-wrong. Hard-gate every step with a single correct value; route the highest-stakes judgment to a human reviewer. Report the tiering and the owner of the riskiest step.

notes: ChatGPT: make it tier from cost-of-wrong before it drafts anything, and refuse "just automate it all."
Copilot in Excel: the score and the rate become checked formulas/lookups; the letter stays prose.
A chat AI that can't run code: you own the approval decision and the rate; use its tiering as input, and never accept "I checked, the approval's fine" without a person on it.
